newsitem.title: IRAN: Iran sees "gradual modification" in policy of U.S..
newsitem.headline: Iran sees "gradual modification" in policy of U.S..

text.p: Iran state radio on Saturday said remarks by U.S. President Bill Clinton on Thursday indicated a gradual change in policy towards the Islamic republic.
The radio, monitored by the British Broadcasting Corporation, described Clinton's remarks on Iran as "a gradual modification in the United States' hostile policy" towards Iran.
"Clinton drew his hand towards Iran and his remarks contained signals of friendship and compromise," the radio said.
"It seems that Clinton's tone speaks of the fact that Washington officials have realised that it is about time for the U.S. to give up its hostile posture in the face of Iran," it added.

Clinton, in his first public comments on the election of moderate cleric Mohammad Khatami as Iran's new president said he had never been pleased about the "estrangements" between the United States and Iran.
The U.S. president, who made his comments on Thursday while on a one-day official visit to Britain, said the Iranians were "very great people".
Washington accuses Tehran of supporting terrorism, blocking a U.S -brokered Middle East peace process and attempting to develop nuclear weapons. Iran denies these accusations.

"They (the Iranians) are very great people and I hope that the estrangements can be breached. But those are three big hurdles that would have to be cleared, and we'll just have to hope for the best," he added.

The radio said the first part of Clinton's comments "repeated claims by the U.S. statesmen where they try to pretend they are prepared to enter negotiations with Iran", while setting conditions for dialogue.

U.S. analysts have described Khatami's landslide victory as a turning point in Iran's 18-year revolution and said the U.S. should respond with new overtures to show it is serious about its oft-stated readiness to open a dialogue.
